Clinical Compass

Final project report · Emma Holub

Clinical Compass takes a new diagnosis and turns it into something a person can actually use: plain language, guideline-linked treatment options with the safety evidence attached, a short list of questions worth bringing to the next appointment, and nearby recruiting trials. It doesn't diagnose and it doesn't recommend. It gets someone ready for the conversation where those things happen.

Repository: github.com/emmaholub/Clinical-Compass · App: clinicalcomp.onrender.com

The thesis: streamline the question, not the decision. A patient who arrives at a fifteen-minute visit already oriented can spend more of that visit discussing what matters to them. Clinical Compass prepares the patient; the clinician still diagnoses, recommends, and decides with them.

Working-plan boundary: this report describes a class-project prototype and a proposed path to a clinically reviewed product. It is not medical or legal advice.

1. Motivation

There's a particular kind of helplessness in holding a word you can't pronounce, knowing it now describes your own body, and having fifteen minutes to make sense of it before the next patient gets called back. That's not a failure of information, because there is more medical information online than any one person could read in a lifetime. It's a failure of translation: nothing sized to someone who isn't a clinician and doesn't have time to become one before Tuesday.

Doctors already know what closing that gap is worth. The literature has a term for it, "patient activation," and it isn't fuzzy: patients who understand their condition tend to stick with treatment longer, report fewer surprises when side effects show up, and leave visits more satisfied with the care itself. None of that requires the patient to know more than their doctor. It requires them to walk in already oriented: roughly what the diagnosis means, what's usually tried first, and what's worth asking about the part that actually worries them.

That's the whole job Clinical Compass is trying to do, and it's a narrower job than it might sound. It explains, it cites, it hands someone three questions before they forget the one that mattered. It does not diagnose, and it does not tell anyone what to take. A physician still does both, exactly as they do today. If the tool is working, nobody notices it in the exam room. They just have a better fifteen minutes.

For the patientA readable explanation, evidence that can be inspected, and questions that make their priorities easier to voice.
For the clinicianA patient who arrives oriented, so scarce visit time can move sooner toward preferences, tradeoffs, monitoring, and decisions.
For safetyA visible boundary: no diagnosis, prescribing, individualized eligibility decision, or second-guessing of the clinician’s plan.

The significance is not that software knows more than a physician. It is that a patient who understands the landscape can participate in a decision that affects their body, schedule, finances, family, and quality of life. If the product helps someone recognize a question they would otherwise miss or stay engaged with a plan they and their clinician chose together, the consequence could be life-changing and, in a serious case, potentially harm-preventing. That is an impact hypothesis to measure, not a life-saving guarantee to advertise.

2. What is new

Most of what already exists for this falls into two buckets: the open web, where a chatbot will answer confidently whether or not it actually knows, and the clinical literature itself, written for people who already have a medical degree. Clinical Compass tries to live in the gap between those two, and it earns that spot the unglamorous way. Every treatment shown is pulled from an actual clinical guideline, not guessed at by a language model. Every drug fact comes from the drug's real FDA label or a published study, not from the model's memory. And before any of it reaches the screen, the exact sentence behind a claim is checked against the live source text. If that check fails, the number doesn't get hedged or softened. It disappears, and the page says, plainly, that it couldn't be verified.

That restraint shows up again in a decision I want to be honest about. The original plan for this product was to rank treatments by how often they're actually prescribed, using a dataset like IQVIA's prescription data or FactSet's StreetAccount Drug Database. I looked into both. Neither is available without an enterprise license, and StreetAccount's own terms of use explicitly prohibit using its data to build another product on top of it. I could have approximated prescribing frequency from public mentions or trial counts and presented it with the same confidence as everything else on the page, and nobody would have known the difference. That's exactly the kind of quiet dishonesty this project exists to push back against, so instead Compass ranks by guideline role: first-line versus alternative, each with real evidence attached, not a number I couldn't stand behind. Section 8 covers what it would actually take to add a licensed prescribing-volume feed later.

Where the product sits

Existing optionStrengthGap Clinical Compass addresses
WebMD, Healthline, Mayo ClinicBroad, familiar health informationUsually generic and not organized around the patient’s next appointment or a traceable treatment-evidence chain.
Ada Health, K Health, BuoyPre-diagnosis symptom guidanceThey operate before a diagnosis; Compass starts after the diagnosis and prepares the next conversation.
ChatGPT itselfFlexible conversation and broad knowledgeIt can answer almost anything, but a general chat does not inherently enforce this product's source hierarchy, URL-specific claim validation, safety layout, doctor-question artifact, or recruiting US trial filters. Compass narrows the task so patients can inspect the evidence chain rather than rely on conversational confidence. See the control test below.
OpenEvidenceEvidence search and clinician-oriented medical answersIts primary audience and workflow are clinical professionals. Compass is designed for a patient or caregiver after a diagnosis, translating the evidence into plain language, questions for the next visit, safety context, and clickable US trial records without pretending to practice medicine.
Hippocratic AIEnterprise patient-facing agentsBroad health-system platform; Compass is a narrow, public-facing education and visit-preparation wedge.
TrialJectory, AntidotePatient clinical-trial matchingCompass keeps trial discovery but connects it to diagnosis orientation, treatment context, safety evidence, and doctor questions.

The competitive question is not whether ChatGPT or OpenEvidence can produce a medical paragraph. They can. The question is whether a patient receives a bounded artifact they can carry into a visit: named public sources, evidence attached to each treatment, safety warnings separated from efficacy, a short list of doctor questions, and official recruiting US trials they can open and inspect. That is the workflow Clinical Compass is built to own.

Product principles carried over from the original proposal: show the treatment landscape rather than declare a winner; end every page with a short question list rather than an answer; make side effects first-class; attach every number to the study or label that produced it; keep prescribing frequency separate from clinical merit; and ensure revenue never changes what appears or how it is ordered. The resulting patient experience is intentionally different from a general chatbot: less conversational improvisation, more bounded evidence and transparent uncertainty.

Control test: the same question in ChatGPT

To test the comparison rather than assert it, I asked ChatGPT (chatgpt.com, logged out, October 24, 2026) the question a newly diagnosed patient would bring to Clinical Compass: “I was just diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. What are my treatment options, how well does each one work, what are the side effects, and what percentage of people stop each drug because of side effects? Are there any clinical trials in the US I could join? Please include sources.” The full verbatim transcript is in the repository at experiments/chatgpt_control/.

ChatGPT's answer was careful and, as far as I could check, accurate. It is a stronger baseline than a web search, and I want to say so plainly. It did not invent discontinuation rates; it declined to give any, writing that a single percentage per drug “would imply more certainty than the evidence supports.” The differences are in what a patient can check and what they leave with.

ChatGPT (one run, October 24, 2026)Clinical Compass (rheumatoid arthritis run, Section 4)
Drug-specific numbersNone. No efficacy or discontinuation figure for any drug, including ones printed on the FDA label.Shows a figure only when a source states it, for example leflunomide's ACR20 (20% improvement in American College of Rheumatology criteria) response of 52% vs. 26% for placebo, from the FDA label. Otherwise shows a labeled gap.
CitationsSource chips per paragraph (for example “PMC +1”, “FDA +1”). No quoted passage tied to a specific claim.Each claim has a “source & exact quote” expander, and the quote is checked against the text at its URL before display.
Unsupported claimsAvoided by withholding numbers.Generated claims are checked; an unsupported leflunomide discontinuation-rate claim was removed (Step 4).
Clinical trials3 recruiting US studies, all verified real on ClinicalTrials.gov. One (NCT05197530) is Phase 1 with 40 participants.Fixed filters: US, recruiting, Phase 2 or later, planned enrollment of at least 100. The Phase 1 study would be excluded.
Doctor questions5 good, general questions.3 disease-specific questions. Comparable value; not a differentiator.
Length and shapeAbout 2,200 words in one reply. Shape depends on how the question is worded.The same structured cards every time, expandable on demand.

Limits of this control: it is one run of one question. ChatGPT's answers vary between runs and with how a question is worded, and a signed-in user with a different model could get a different answer.

3. The agents

Underneath the page, a boss agent takes whatever the patient actually typed, misspelled or abbreviated, however a real person types when they're not thinking about data entry ("RA," "T2D"), and cleans it up before anything else runs. From there it fans out to five workers, each built around a single question a patient would actually ask, rather than one worker trying to do all of it in a single enormous prompt.

I split the work this finely for a specific reason: when one agent tries to cover overview, safety, and alternatives all at once, a bad answer about side effects can hide inside an otherwise confident-sounding paragraph, and nobody downstream notices. Keeping each worker narrow means a failure stays loud and local instead of getting smoothed over. Every worker returns a strict, typed model rather than a free-text blob the frontend has to interpret, and the model itself, Portkey-routed gpt-6-luna for this submission, is told explicitly to treat anything it retrieves from the internet as data to read, not instructions to follow. I chose that course-approved model because it keeps the project within the course budget while supporting structured outputs, parallel workers, and bounded response time. The model is an organizer and translator, never the source of a clinical fact. Timeouts, a two-request ceiling per extraction, and a hard cap on evidence lookups per drug keep one bad run from turning into an expensive or endless one.

Why the architecture is a business decision: a narrow worker makes failures attributable, source checks auditable, and costs bounded. The system is allowed to return a partial result. When evidence cannot be verified, the UI says “Not reported” or explains what failed instead of filling the gap with a polished guess. That is the trust mechanism that makes the product meaningfully different from a fluent but untraceable chatbot.

4. Real run: rheumatoid arthritis

What follows is one real lookup against the deployed app, screenshot by screenshot, in the order an actual patient would see it, not a mockup, not a happy-path cherry-pick, just what the app returned.

Every US clinical-trial card is clickable. Clicking See details & contact the team opens the underlying official ClinicalTrials.gov record. This preserves the source of truth and lets a patient or caregiver inspect the sponsor, US locations, eligibility criteria, recruitment status, contacts, and full study details there. Clinical Compass surfaces candidates, while the study team confirms individual eligibility and whether a local site has an opening.
The opt-in is a public-good feature, not a surveillance feature. The search form says “Help improve Clinical Compass with anonymous daily counts of condition lookups.” If enabled, it records only one aggregate count per canonical condition per day. No account, IP address, browser identifier, raw search history, or medical results. That signal cannot prove disease prevalence or product effectiveness, but it can show where people are seeking help so the team can prioritize clinician-reviewed pages, translations, accessibility, and outreach.
Run evidence: the three representative live lookups used for the tokenomics check returned structured usage records. The run outputs were captured locally while the page was assembled. The Portkey dashboard also supplies aggregate billing evidence for the account window shown below.

5. Tokenomics

If this is going to stay free for the people using it, the cost per lookup has to actually hold up, not just sound reasonable in a plan. A few choices keep it in check: every structured extraction is capped at two LLM requests, evidence lookups are cached for 24 hours so the same question isn't paid for twice, the five workers run concurrently instead of one after another, and each worker's prompt carries only the documents it personally needs, not the full pile of evidence gathered for the whole page.

Performance and cost tradeoff

The cost controls were designed to protect both response time and correctness. Wave 1 workers run concurrently, Wave 2 waits for the verified drug list, each structured extraction has at most two model requests, evidence is cached for 24 hours, each drug has a shared ceiling of ten evidence HTTP attempts, and section timeouts range from 60 to 110 seconds. Those controls bound spend, but they can also produce partial results when a source is slow or a claim fails validation. That is a deliberate tradeoff: a shorter answer with an honest missing-data note is safer than an impressive answer with an unsupported number.

Type 2 diabetes21 seconds7Returned populated sections after one validation retry. The retry increased cost, but protected the page from an invalid claim.
Alzheimer's12.1 seconds6Returned the same major patient-facing sections in a separate disease lookup.
TestedWhat cost cutting did and did not prove: these three runs show that the bounded design can return a complete patient-facing page for representative conditions. They do not prove that every optimization is harmless, because no uncapped baseline or randomized A/B comparison was run. The next performance test should compare the bounded pipeline with a less constrained baseline on completion rate, validated claim count, elapsed time, and cost. For this submission, the observed retry and honest partial-result behavior are the available correctness evidence.

6. Safety

A tool that explains medical evidence to someone in a vulnerable moment doesn't get to be wrong quietly. Each of the following exists because I thought through a specific way this could hurt someone, not as a checklist filled in after the fact.

  • Prompt injection. Every page of retrieved evidence is passed to the model as explicitly untrusted data, with an instruction never to follow directions found inside a source document. A patient's safety shouldn't depend on what a scraped web page happened to say to the model in passing.
  • Unsupported medical claims. Every number and quote shown to the patient is checked against the live text at its cited URL before it renders; an unsupported claim becomes null and shows "Not reported" instead of a guess. Section 4, Step 4 shows this firing for real. A discontinuation-rate claim for leflunomide got generated, failed the check, and was pulled before a patient ever saw it.
  • Wrong-label risk. The brand or innovator label is preferred over a generic one, since generic formulations can differ in ways that matter; combination-drug products are excluded from single-drug searches so a patient isn't shown warnings for a drug they're not taking; and DailyMed is used as a fallback only when an openFDA label can't be found at all.
  • Side-effect overload. Safety is structured in three tiers: FDA boxed warning first, common label-reported reactions with natural-frequency bands second, and discontinuation due to side effects when a pivotal study actually reports it. FAERS stays secondary and expandable because voluntary reports are useful for signal detection but cannot establish incidence or causation.
  • Agent malfunction and overspending. Each worker carries its own timeout (60 to 110 seconds depending on the section), each structured extraction is capped at two LLM requests, each drug has a shared ceiling of ten evidence HTTP attempts, and an anonymous per-connection rate limit bounds how fast one visitor can trigger new lookups.

Liability posture. The boundary is the first control: education and visit preparation, not diagnosis or treatment selection. Before a real clinical launch, the remaining exposure would need a clinician-review sign-off workflow, a clear patient acknowledgment, a hospital Business Associate Agreement where applicable, and technology errors-and-omissions/cyber coverage reviewed by health-tech counsel. These controls reduce risk; they do not make the product immune from liability.

TestedSafety evidence in the repository: the automated suite exercises both worker waves, source validation, wrong-label prevention, unknown diseases, request limits, and partial failures. The rheumatoid arthritis run also shows the validator removing an unsupported discontinuation-rate claim before it reached the patient page. 7. Impact

ObservedInformal user testing. People who tried the live app gave positive feedback on its clarity and ease of use. This is qualitative feedback, not a clinical-outcome study or a timed comparison.
User voiceAnonymous informal tester: “This is really cool and super easy to use. I like that it gives me clear information and questions to bring to my doctor instead of making me search through a bunch of medical websites.”

There is a serious evidence-backed reason to pursue the product beyond a good first reaction. In one cohort, patients with inadequate health literacy were about twice as likely to be hospitalized at least once as patients with adequate literacy (Williams et al., 1998). In a 2015 Health Affairs study of more than 32,000 patients, those who sustained the highest activation in their own care had projected costs 31% lower than those who stayed at the lowest level (Fairview / Health Affairs summary). These studies establish the opportunity, not causation by Clinical Compass. The current product evidence is qualitative validation plus working live runs, not proof of a clinical outcome.

Observed nowInformal testers gave positive feedback on clarity and ease of use. The deployed prototype also produced populated pages for rheumatoid arthritis, type 2 diabetes, and Alzheimer's.
Next patient metricTime to create three concrete questions, plus confidence before and after using the site and whether the questions are actually used in the next visit.
Public-good metricWith optional consent, anonymous daily condition counts can show where people are seeking help and guide clinician review, translation, accessibility, and outreach priorities.

The impact is potentially broader than one better appointment. A free tool could help more people arrive prepared, especially those who cannot spend hours sorting through medical websites. If a patient notices a question or warning sign sooner, finds a legitimate trial to discuss, or stays engaged with a plan they and their clinician chose together, the result could be life-changing and, in some cases, potentially harm-preventing. That is the ambition. Early feedback is encouraging; the next measurement step is a timed, consent-based test of whether the tool changes how patients prepare for and participate in the visit.

8. Limits and next steps

Limits. Guideline retrieval currently leans on UK NICE recommendations (cached, plus a live NICE/PubMed fallback for diseases without a cached URL), and US and UK guidance can genuinely differ, this is not a comprehensive US guideline database, and I don't want to overstate what it covers. Published-evidence retrieval reaches PubMed abstracts and FDA label clinical-study sections, not the full paywalled literature, so a missing finding means "not verified in what was retrieved," not "doesn't exist." FAERS counts are voluntary adverse-event reports, not incidence rates or proof that a drug caused anything. And no tool here determines individual trial eligibility, a study team still has to do that, every time.

Next steps. The one I care about most is a licensed prescribing-volume source, IQVIA NPA/NSPI, or an equivalent dataset with a redistribution right, to finally answer the "which treatment is actually prescribed most" question this product was originally built around, honestly instead of approximately. Past that: broader US guideline coverage beyond NICE, a persistent rate-limit store instead of the process-local one that resets on redeploy, a clinician review pass before this is presented as validated for real use, and a structured, timed follow-up study that builds on the informal user testing already done. None of that is far-fetched work. It's the difference between a project that explains itself well and a product someone's doctor would actually recommend.

Appendix: path from prototype to product

Business model. The product stays free to hospitals and the public, which makes a pilot easy to approve. Revenue would come later from performance-based contracts with payers or health systems, paid only after measurable outcomes such as better medication engagement or fewer avoidable follow-up calls, never from selling patient data. HIPAA's rules on selling protected health information, hospital Business Associate Agreements, and the GoodRx and Flo Health enforcement actions make data sale both legally risky and self-defeating. No pharmaceutical company, pharmacy benefit manager, insurer, or sponsor can pay to change treatment ordering or evidence visibility.

PhaseTimingWorkExit gate
0 · ConciergeMonths 0 to 4Hand-build 5 to 10 clinician-reviewed pages in one narrow disease area; test the question list with real patients.Patients use the questions in a visit and a physician confirms it saved or improved visit time.
1 · PipelineMonths 4 to 10Expand retrieval and validation, add a human sign-off queue, finalize legal review.Time to publish a new page falls from days to hours without losing clinician sign-off.
2 · DistributionMonths 10 to 18Land one free hospital pilot; open a performance-based conversation with one payer.Signed hospital pilot plus a payer letter of intent.
Bottom line: Clinical Compass does not win by pretending to replace care. It wins if it becomes the trustworthy layer between a diagnosis and the next conversation, free enough to reach broadly, disciplined enough to deserve trust, and measurable enough to prove value.
